A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.

bivy.name: Holden Village
bivy.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months
bivy.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.

bivy.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
bivy.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party
bivy.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
bivy.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
bivy.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. bivy.name: Holden Lake
bivy.capacity: Several established sites spread around the basin, enough for a few parties, but they are the obvious base for every Bonanza attempt so expect company in July and August
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and its inlet streams, plus snowmelt high into the summer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in at the trailhead. bivy.name: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above
bivy.capacity: A handful of small pitches at the pass, and higher up only ledges — one or two tents at best above the pass, and parties frequently sleep two to a ledge

bivy.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds

bivy.name: Holden Village
bivy.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months
bivy.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks

bivy.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
bivy.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party
bivy.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
bivy.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. bivy.name: Holden Lake
bivy.capacity: Several established sites spread around the basin, enough for a few parties, but they are the obvious base for every Bonanza attempt so expect company in July and August
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and its inlet streams, plus snowmelt high into the summer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in at the trailhead. Camping and campfires are both prohibited within 200 feet of the lakeshore, which is enforced and is the reason the good sites sit back in the trees and benches. Group size limits apply. Getting here at all depends on the ferry, the bus and the Railroad Creek road being open.

bivy.name: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above
bivy.capacity: A handful of small pitches at the pass, and higher up only ledges — one or two tents at best above the pass, and parties frequently sleep two to a ledge
bivy.water: Snowmelt and running water off the slabs early in the season; by late summer this can dry up entirely and you may have to carry water from Holden Lake
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit. No campfires at this elevation on bare ground and in fragile alpine terrain — carry a stove. Camp on rock, snow or existing bare ground rather than on the heather benches, which do not recover.

The trade is comfort and water for time: an early start off wet slabs in the dark from the pass is a very different proposition to the same ground at first light, so choose the higher camp only if the party is competent moving on that terrain unlit. Exposed to weather with nothing to hide behind.

bivy.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
bivy.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

bivy.name: Holden Lake
bivy.capacity: Several established sites spread around the basin, enough for a few parties, but they are the obvious base for every Bonanza attempt so expect company in July and August

bivy.name: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above

Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.

bivy.name: Holden Village
bivy.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months
bivy.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. Rates are per person per night and include all meals, with a lower long-stay rate and a higher rate in the peak weeks of high summer. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.
bivy.notes: This is the base for Bonanza, Copper, Dumbell's eastern side, and the Railroad Creek walk in to Hart and Lyman Lakes. Its unusual value to a climber is that you can sleep indoors and eat three meals at 3,200 ft the night before starting up a 9,500 ft peak, which no other approach in this zone offers. The catch is that the whole thing runs on a schedule you do not control: a passenger ferry roughly forty miles up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, then a bus about ten miles up a single forest road, with the bus historically running only on certain days. Miss a boat and you lose a day at each end, so the practical trip length is dictated by the sailing schedule rather than by the climb. As of the 2026 season the village is CLOSED to all guests including hikers and the road up Railroad Creek is closed by order after December 2025 flooding and slides destroyed sections of it — using the Lucerne dock or travelling that road in any form is prohibited while the order stands, repairs are expensive and slow, and reopening may slip beyond 2026. Treat any Bonanza plan as unbookable until that order is lifted, and confirm directly rather than assuming a summer has reopened it.

bivy.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
bivy.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party
bivy.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
bivy.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Reaching it at all depends on the ferry and the Railroad Creek road, so the ferry booking is the real constraint. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
bivy.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. Being an open field it is exposed and has no shelter, and with only a site or two you cannot count on it if another party arrived on the same boat. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. It is subject to exactly the same road closure as the village — while Railroad Creek road is closed by order there is no legal way to reach it.

bivy.name: Holden Lake
bivy.capacity: Several established sites spread around the basin, enough for a few parties, but they are the obvious base for every Bonanza attempt so expect company in July and August
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and its inlet streams, plus snowmelt high into the summer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in at the trailhead. Camping and campfires are both prohibited within 200 feet of the lakeshore, which is enforced and is the reason the good sites sit back in the trees and benches. Group size limits apply. Getting here at all depends on the ferry, the bus and the Railroad Creek road being open.
bivy.notes: This is the standard base camp for Bonanza Peak and the natural place to sleep before the Mary Green Glacier, the Northeast Buttress or the North Ridge. The trail leaves the Railroad Creek valley at around 3,600 ft and climbs four miles of switchbacks to the lake, which puts most of the day's work behind you before the climbing starts. From here a typical Mary Green day is around eleven hours camp to camp with several thousand feet of gain, so parties either accept a long day from the lake or push a high camp higher. It is also the launching point for Martin Peak and for traverses toward Holden Pass. The whole basin is remote enough that self-rescue is the realistic plan — there is no road within a day of you, and the way out is a boat.

bivy.name: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above
bivy.capacity: A handful of small pitches at the pass, and higher up only ledges — one or two tents at best above the pass, and parties frequently sleep two to a ledge
bivy.water: Snowmelt and running water off the slabs early in the season; by late summer this can dry up entirely and you may have to carry water from Holden Lake
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit. No campfires at this elevation on bare ground and in fragile alpine terrain — carry a stove. Camp on rock, snow or existing bare ground rather than on the heather benches, which do not recover.
bivy.notes: Holden Pass at about 6,400 ft is the higher option for Bonanza and cuts a serious amount off summit day compared with sleeping at the lake. Parties who want more push another five hundred feet to ledges below the waterfall slabs at roughly 6,900 ft, which is a genuine bivouac rather than a campsite and is worth scouting in daylight before committing to it in the dark. From either, the route makes a rising traverse west to the snowfield below the slabs, scrambles onto the northern edge of the Mary Green Glacier and works southwest under the northeast ridge. The trade is comfort and water for time: an early start off wet slabs in the dark from the pass is a very different proposition to the same ground at first light, so choose the higher camp only if the party is competent moving on that terrain unlit. Exposed to weather with nothing to hide behind.

bivy.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
bivy.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing
bivy.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west it needs a Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass at the Phelps Creek trailhead; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
bivy.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk. Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.

bivy.name: Spider Meadow and Phelps Basin
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites through a mile-long meadow, plus quieter ground in Phelps Basin above it — the meadow absorbs a lot of parties but is genuinely busy on summer weekends
bivy.water: Reliable — Phelps Creek runs the length of the meadow and the basin above holds snowmelt streams well into the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead, which is entered about two and a half miles up. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at Phelps Creek. Camp on established bare sites rather than in the meadow itself, and expect fire restrictions from midsummer onward on top of the usual high-elevation limits.
bivy.notes: About five and a half miles and 1,250 ft from the Phelps Creek trailhead at roughly 3,500 ft, this is the standard first night for almost everything on the Chiwawa side. It stages the Spider Gap crossing to Lyman Lakes and so serves North Star, Cloudy and Chiwawa; Phelps Basin half a mile above the head of the meadow is the base for Dumbell Mountain, whose route climbs northwest out of the upper basin, steepens around 6,100 ft and works up talus and a weakness to the notch west of the summit. Higher bivouac ground exists at Larch Knob, about 1,600 ft above the meadow on the switchbacks toward Spider Gap, with a few platforms partly sheltered from the wind pouring through the gap. The same trailhead also serves the Carne Mountain trail, whose basin at about 6,100 ft holds several camps with good water and is the link to the saddle above Ice Lakes and across to Leroy — those saddle camps have no water other than snowmelt. Road access is the weak point here: the Chiwawa River road is long, the final twelve miles are rough gravel unfriendly to low clearance, and the last two miles of the Phelps Creek spur are rougher still.

bivy.name: Leroy Basin
bivy.capacity: Several established sites in a flat basin, comfortably a few parties, and the standard climbers' base for this side of the crest
bivy.water: Reliable — clear streams through the basin, though upper snowfields are what feed them and a very late-season camp may need to walk down for water
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful at the trailhead. No campfires this high — carry a stove. Use the existing sites; the basin is small and the meadow ground scars quickly.
bivy.notes: This is the climbers' basin for Mount Maude and Seven Fingered Jack from the west, and it is also the base most parties use for Mount Fernow. Reach it by hiking about three miles up the Phelps Creek trail, fording Leroy Creek at around 4,140 ft, then taking the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the north side of the creek to the flat at 6,100 ft. The ford is the crux of the approach rather than an afterthought: Leroy Creek runs high and fast through early summer and often does not settle until August, so an early-season party should plan the crossing for morning and be prepared to turn round. From camp, Seven Fingered Jack's southwest slopes and Maude's south side are both reasonable days, and the two are frequently combined. Maude's north-side lines, including the ice fall and the couloir, are a different proposition entirely and are approached from the far side of the peak. Larch colour makes this a heavily visited basin in the first half of October.

bivy.name: Ice Lakes
bivy.capacity: Established sites on benches and pumice flats around both lakes; the upper lake takes a fair number of tents in season and the lower lake has room, though the peninsula on the lower lake is closed to camping
bivy.water: Reliable — both lakes, with inlet snowmelt through most of the summer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass at the Entiat River trailhead. Campfires are prohibited within half a mile of the Ice Lakes, so a stove is mandatory here. Camp on the pumice flats and bare benches rather than the fragile meadow, and honour the closure on the lower lake's peninsula.
bivy.notes: This is the eastern base for Mount Maude, and the reason Maude and Seven Fingered Jack are two-sided objectives rather than Phelps Creek peaks. It is a long way in — roughly fourteen miles of Entiat River trail from the road end at Cottonwood Campground at about 3,140 ft, then a rough side path climbing through boulders for another mile and a half or two to the upper lake, with the upper lake sitting about a mile and four hundred feet above the lower one, directly under Maude's face. From the upper lake Maude's shoulder is a walk-up by the standards of this range. The same valley head serves the Entiat Meadows under Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Maude, and Buckskin Mountain sits on the divide above, reachable either from here or from Copper Basin on the Holden side, which is also how Copper Peak is normally climbed. The whole Entiat corridor has burned repeatedly and much of the trail is exposed, dry and dusty with little shade and no reliable water between the river and the lakes. In 2026 a very large fire in this valley destroyed structures and closed the trail and road outright for months; assume nothing about access here without checking, and expect standing dead timber and blowdown for years afterwards.

bivy.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
bivy.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
bivy.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
bivy.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.

bivy.name: Lena Lake designated sites
bivy.capacity: Large by Olympic standards — roughly 28 to 29 numbered sites strung along the west and north shores, with a couple more on the east side; two pit toilets. It is the biggest backcountry camp in this zone and it still fills on summer weekends
bivy.water: Reliable. The lake itself, and the inlet creeks at the north end. Filter or treat everything — this is a heavily used shoreline
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass required to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit, no reservation and no fee for the sites themselves — it is Forest Service ground, first come first served. Camping is restricted to the numbered sites. Wilderness rules apply once you leave the lake basin: stoves only, no campfires, and a party limit of twelve. Plan on cooking on a stove at the lake as well
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the whole Hamma Hamma side and the single most useful site in this zone. Three easy miles and about 1,300 ft of gain on a wide graded trail from the road, so a party can leave the car after work and be in camp before dark, which is exactly how most Brothers and Mount Stone trips are staged. From here two entirely separate objectives open up: north into the Valley of the Silent Men for The Brothers, and west and up for Upper Lena Lake and the traverse toward Mount Stone. Being outside Olympic National Park is the point — no quota, no reservation, no fee, so it is the fallback when the park permits above it are gone. The cost is crowding and noise; this is a family backpacking destination as much as a climbers' camp, and the shoreline shows it. Snow-free and usable most of the year, which makes it a genuine early-season and late-season base when everything higher is buried.

bivy.name: The Brothers climbers camp, Valley of the Silent Men
bivy.capacity: A scatter of flat, obvious tent spots in old-growth forest beside the creek, generally reported at around half a dozen usable pitches, informal rather than numbered
bivy.water: Reliable while the creek runs. The East Fork of Lena Creek is right beside the pitches, and this is the last dependable water — carry everything you need for the climb from here, because the couloir and the upper mountain hold none
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit or fee — this is inside The Brothers Wilderness on Forest Service land, not in the national park. Wilderness regulations bind: STOVES ONLY, no campfires at all, party limit of twelve, and gathering wood above 3,500 ft is prohibited outright. Practise strict Leave No Trace, the camp has no toilet
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for The Brothers and the reason the traverse between the north and south peaks is a two-day trip rather than a brutal one. Reached by continuing past the north end of Lena Lake, crossing the inlet and following the East Fork up the Valley of the Silent Men through mossy old growth — call it three miles and 1,200 ft beyond the lake, so about six miles and 2,300 ft total from the car. From camp the south couloir rises directly above, and the summit day is short enough to allow an early start and a return to the tents before the couloir softens. It is a forest camp, not an alpine one: no views, damp, and the mosquitoes are memorable in early summer. The couloir is the season-limiting factor rather than the camp — good neve through late spring and early summer, loose and unpleasant once it melts out, so most parties come between April and early July and bring an axe and crampons.

bivy.name: Upper Lena Lake
bivy.capacity: Eight designated wilderness sites in the meadow basin, and that is the hard ceiling — the basin is small, fragile and closely managed
bivy.water: Reliable. The lake, plus meltwater in the basin early in the season. This is the last certain water before the high traverse toward Scout Lake and St. Peter's Gate
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED, AND THIS IS A NAMED QUOTA AREA — the boundary is crossed on the climb up from Lena Lake, so the rules change midway. Reserve through Recreation.gov, choosing Staircase as the entry area and Upper Lena Lake as the camp; the reservation season runs roughly July into mid-October and permits for the summer are released in a single April window that clears quickly. Per-person nightly fees apply on top of a booking fee. An animal-resistant food container is required throughout the park wilderness. No campfires — well above the 3,500 ft fire limit. A Northwest Forest Pass is still needed at the trailhead, because the parking is on Forest Service ground
bivy.notes: The high camp for the northern approach to Mount Stone. Seven-odd miles and around 3,900 ft from the Lena Lake trailhead, of which the last three miles above the lower lake are steep and rooty and feel far longer than the distance suggests. From here the traverse runs southwest past Scout Lake to St. Peter's Gate, the notch under Mount Stone, and parties often continue over the gate and out via Lake of the Angels and the Putvin trail, which needs a car shuttle between two Hamma Hamma trailheads. Getting the permit is the whole planning problem: eight sites against considerable demand means the reservation window matters more than the weather. If it is gone, camp at Lena Lake below and accept a much longer summit day, or come at Mount Stone from the Putvin side instead. Snow lingers in the basin into July in a heavy year, and the meadow is the reason the sites are designated — stay on them.

bivy.name: Lake of the Angels
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites in the upper basin. Four. It is a small hanging meadow and there is no overflow ground that is acceptable to camp on
bivy.water: The lake, but READ THIS ONE CAREFULLY. It is a shallow basin lake fed by snowmelt with no significant inlet, so it draws down through the summer and by a dry late season it can be low, warm and unappealing, and the meadow seeps around it disappear entirely. There is a good spring roughly two miles up the Putvin trail that is often the last dependable water on a dry year. Late-season parties should plan to carry water up from lower on the trail rather than count on finding it in the basin
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED — the trail crosses the park boundary shortly before the final climb into the basin, having already passed through the Mount Skokomish Wilderness on Forest Service ground below. Book through Recreation.gov or obtain the permit from a park wilderness information office; per-person nightly fees apply. An animal-resistant food container is required. NO CAMPFIRES — the basin is far above the 3,500 ft fire limit and this is stove-only ground. No dogs. No Northwest Forest Pass or other parking pass is needed at the Putvin trailhead itself, which is unusual for this road and worth knowing
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Skokomish and for the south side of Mount Stone, and one of the best-placed camps in the Olympics for a climber. About 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft from the Putvin trailhead, which understates it badly — the trail is notoriously steep, with hand-over-hand sections on rock and root where a slip has real consequence, and it is slow going with an overnight pack. From the basin the east slopes of Mount Skokomish are a straightforward scramble, and Mount Stone is gained by working north toward St. Peter's Gate, so a fit party can take both peaks in one day from these tents. The four sites and the meadow are the constraint: this is a fragile alpine basin that has been loved hard, so camp only on the designated ground and expect company. Best from mid-July, once the steep upper trail is clear of snow, through September. Early season the last pitch to the basin holds snow and the trail is genuinely hazardous when wet.

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations
bivy.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.

bivy.name: Jefferson Creek roadside pull-outs, FR 2401
bivy.capacity: Informal — a handful of turnouts and flat spots along the spur near where the road crosses Jefferson Creek. No facilities of any kind, no toilet, no table
bivy.water: Jefferson Creek at the crossing, filtered. Nothing above it on the climb, so fill here
bivy.permit: Dispersed camping on Olympic National Forest roads needs no permit and no fee, but it is bound by the usual rules: stay within about 150 ft of the road centreline on a road open to it, camp well back from water, pack everything out, and observe the fourteen-day stay limit. Check the district motor vehicle use map before relying on a particular spur, since some roads are seasonally gated or closed to camping. Fire restrictions are common in late summer and are worth confirming
bivy.notes: This is the staging spot for MOUNT PERSHING and effectively nothing else, which is why it earns a line despite being a patch of gravel. The route starts where FR 2401 crosses Jefferson Creek at around 2,400 ft, reached by leaving FR 25 for FR 2480 and then FR 2401, and there is no trailhead, no sign and no established camp — a faint flagged path on the north side of the creek is the whole infrastructure. Sleeping at the crossing turns a long drive on rough gravel plus a steep bushwhack and class 3 ridge into a manageable day. Treat the road itself as the main uncertainty: the Jefferson Creek spurs are lightly maintained, subject to washouts and blowdown, and a low-clearance car may not reach the crossing at all, in which case the walk gets considerably longer. There is no water and no shelter once you leave here.

bivy.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
bivy.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a NORTHWEST FOREST PASS IS REQUIRED AT THE MOUNT ELLINOR UPPER TRAILHEAD BUT NOT AT THE LOWER ONE, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
bivy.notes: The obvious roadside base for MOUNT ELLINOR AND MOUNT WASHINGTON, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is EXPLICITLY A CONTINGENCY RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.

bivy.name: Staircase Campground, North Fork Skokomish
bivy.capacity: Around 49 sites along the river, some reservable in high summer and the rest first come, first served
bivy.water: Potable water in season; the North Fork Skokomish runs through the campground
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park entrance fee applies, plus a per-night campground fee. Reservations through Recreation.gov are used for the peak midsummer window and the campground reverts to first come, first served either side of it; it runs primitive with reduced services through the winter. NO WILDERNESS PERMIT IS NEEDED FOR THE CAMPGROUND ITSELF — that is only for backcountry nights. Standard park food storage rules apply. Access is by the unpaved FR 24 beyond Lake Cushman, which closes in bad weather and is frequently shut through the winter and spring
bivy.notes: The park-side alternative at the head of Lake Cushman, a few miles beyond Big Creek. For the climbing in this zone it is a SECOND-CHOICE CONTINGENCY rather than a plan: it is further from the Ellinor and Washington trailheads than Big Creek, it costs more because of the park entrance fee, and the road in is less dependable. It earns its place for two reasons. It is the entry area named on the permit for Upper Lena Lake, so a party collecting or sorting out a park wilderness permit may already be dealing with this side of the boundary. And it is the fallback with real amenities when the Forest Service campgrounds below Ellinor are full on a summer weekend, which they routinely are. Worth knowing that the developed area has had extended seasonal closures in recent years, so confirm it is open before committing to the drive.

bivy.name: Lena Lake designated sites
bivy.capacity: Large by Olympic standards — roughly 28 to 29 numbered sites strung along the west and north shores, with a couple more on the east side; two pit toilets. It is the biggest backcountry camp in this zone and it still fills on summer weekends
bivy.water: Reliable. The lake itself, and the inlet creeks at the north end. Filter or treat everything — this is a heavily used shoreline
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass required to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit, no reservation and no fee for the sites themselves — it is Forest Service ground, first come first served. Camping is restricted to the numbered sites. Wilderness rules apply once you leave the lake basin: stoves only, no campfires, and a party limit of twelve. Plan on cooking on a stove at the lake as well
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the whole Hamma Hamma side and the single most useful site in this zone. Three easy miles and about 1,300 ft of gain on a wide graded trail from the road, so a party can leave the car after work and be in camp before dark, which is exactly how most Brothers and Mount Stone trips are staged. From here two entirely separate objectives open up: north into the Valley of the Silent Men for The Brothers, and west and up for Upper Lena Lake and the traverse toward Mount Stone. Being outside Olympic National Park is the point — no quota, no reservation, no fee, so it is the fallback when the park permits above it are gone. The cost is crowding and noise; this is a family backpacking destination as much as a climbers' camp, and the shoreline shows it. Snow-free and usable most of the year, which makes it a genuine early-season and late-season base when everything higher is buried.

bivy.name: The Brothers climbers camp, Valley of the Silent Men
bivy.capacity: A scatter of flat, obvious tent spots in old-growth forest beside the creek, generally reported at around half a dozen usable pitches, informal rather than numbered
bivy.water: Reliable while the creek runs. The East Fork of Lena Creek is right beside the pitches, and this is the last dependable water — carry everything you need for the climb from here, because the couloir and the upper mountain hold none
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit or fee — this is inside The Brothers Wilderness on Forest Service land, not in the national park. Wilderness regulations bind: STOVES ONLY, no campfires at all, party limit of twelve, and gathering wood above 3,500 ft is prohibited outright. Practise strict Leave No Trace, the camp has no toilet
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for The Brothers and the reason the traverse between the north and south peaks is a two-day trip rather than a brutal one. Reached by continuing past the north end of Lena Lake, crossing the inlet and following the East Fork up the Valley of the Silent Men through mossy old growth — call it three miles and 1,200 ft beyond the lake, so about six miles and 2,300 ft total from the car. From camp the south couloir rises directly above, and the summit day is short enough to allow an early start and a return to the tents before the couloir softens. It is a forest camp, not an alpine one: no views, damp, and the mosquitoes are memorable in early summer. The couloir is the season-limiting factor rather than the camp — good neve through late spring and early summer, loose and unpleasant once it melts out, so most parties come between April and early July and bring an axe and crampons.

bivy.name: Upper Lena Lake
bivy.capacity: Eight designated wilderness sites in the meadow basin, and that is the hard ceiling — the basin is small, fragile and closely managed
bivy.water: Reliable. The lake, plus meltwater in the basin early in the season. This is the last certain water before the high traverse toward Scout Lake and St. Peter's Gate
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED, AND THIS IS A NAMED QUOTA AREA — the boundary is crossed on the climb up from Lena Lake, so the rules change midway. Reserve through Recreation.gov, choosing Staircase as the entry area and Upper Lena Lake as the camp; the reservation season runs roughly July into mid-October and permits for the summer are released in a single April window that clears quickly. Per-person nightly fees apply on top of a booking fee. An animal-resistant food container is required throughout the park wilderness. No campfires — well above the 3,500 ft fire limit. A Northwest Forest Pass is still needed at the trailhead, because the parking is on Forest Service ground
bivy.notes: The high camp for the northern approach to Mount Stone. Seven-odd miles and around 3,900 ft from the Lena Lake trailhead, of which the last three miles above the lower lake are steep and rooty and feel far longer than the distance suggests. From here the traverse runs southwest past Scout Lake to St. Peter's Gate, the notch under Mount Stone, and parties often continue over the gate and out via Lake of the Angels and the Putvin trail, which needs a car shuttle between two Hamma Hamma trailheads. Getting the permit is the whole planning problem: eight sites against considerable demand means the reservation window matters more than the weather. If it is gone, camp at Lena Lake below and accept a much longer summit day, or come at Mount Stone from the Putvin side instead. Snow lingers in the basin into July in a heavy year, and the meadow is the reason the sites are designated — stay on them.

bivy.name: Lake of the Angels
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites in the upper basin. Four. It is a small hanging meadow and there is no overflow ground that is acceptable to camp on
bivy.water: The lake, but READ THIS ONE CAREFULLY. It is a shallow basin lake fed by snowmelt with no significant inlet, so it draws down through the summer and by a dry late season it can be low, warm and unappealing, and the meadow seeps around it disappear entirely. There is a good spring roughly two miles up the Putvin trail that is often the last dependable water on a dry year. Late-season parties should plan to carry water up from lower on the trail rather than count on finding it in the basin
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED — the trail crosses the park boundary shortly before the final climb into the basin, having already passed through the Mount Skokomish Wilderness on Forest Service ground below. Book through Recreation.gov or obtain the permit from a park wilderness information office; per-person nightly fees apply. An animal-resistant food container is required. NO CAMPFIRES — the basin is far above the 3,500 ft fire limit and this is stove-only ground. No dogs. No Northwest Forest Pass or other parking pass is needed at the Putvin trailhead itself, which is unusual for this road and worth knowing
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Skokomish and for the south side of Mount Stone, and one of the best-placed camps in the Olympics for a climber. About 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft from the Putvin trailhead, which understates it badly — the trail is notoriously steep, with hand-over-hand sections on rock and root where a slip has real consequence, and it is slow going with an overnight pack. From the basin the east slopes of Mount Skokomish are a straightforward scramble, and Mount Stone is gained by working north toward St. Peter's Gate, so a fit party can take both peaks in one day from these tents. The four sites and the meadow are the constraint: this is a fragile alpine basin that has been loved hard, so camp only on the designated ground and expect company. Best from mid-July, once the steep upper trail is clear of snow, through September. Early season the last pitch to the basin holds snow and the trail is genuinely hazardous when wet.

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations
bivy.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.

bivy.name: Jefferson Creek roadside pull-outs, FR 2401
bivy.capacity: Informal — a handful of turnouts and flat spots along the spur near where the road crosses Jefferson Creek. No facilities of any kind, no toilet, no table
bivy.water: Jefferson Creek at the crossing, filtered. Nothing above it on the climb, so fill here
bivy.permit: Dispersed camping on Olympic National Forest roads needs no permit and no fee, but it is bound by the usual rules: stay within about 150 ft of the road centreline on a road open to it, camp well back from water, pack everything out, and observe the fourteen-day stay limit. Check the district motor vehicle use map before relying on a particular spur, since some roads are seasonally gated or closed to camping. Fire restrictions are common in late summer and are worth confirming
bivy.notes: This is the staging spot for MOUNT PERSHING and effectively nothing else, which is why it earns a line despite being a patch of gravel. The route starts where FR 2401 crosses Jefferson Creek at around 2,400 ft, reached by leaving FR 25 for FR 2480 and then FR 2401, and there is no trailhead, no sign and no established camp — a faint flagged path on the north side of the creek is the whole infrastructure. Sleeping at the crossing turns a long drive on rough gravel plus a steep bushwhack and class 3 ridge into a manageable day. Treat the road itself as the main uncertainty: the Jefferson Creek spurs are lightly maintained, subject to washouts and blowdown, and a low-clearance car may not reach the crossing at all, in which case the walk gets considerably longer. There is no water and no shelter once you leave here.

bivy.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
bivy.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a NORTHWEST FOREST PASS IS REQUIRED AT THE MOUNT ELLINOR UPPER TRAILHEAD BUT NOT AT THE LOWER ONE, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
bivy.notes: The obvious roadside base for MOUNT ELLINOR AND MOUNT WASHINGTON, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is EXPLICITLY A CONTINGENCY RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.

bivy.name: Staircase Campground, North Fork Skokomish
bivy.capacity: Around 49 sites along the river, some reservable in high summer and the rest first come, first served
bivy.water: Potable water in season; the North Fork Skokomish runs through the campground
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park entrance fee applies, plus a per-night campground fee. Reservations through Recreation.gov are used for the peak midsummer window and the campground reverts to first come, first served either side of it; it runs primitive with reduced services through the winter. NO WILDERNESS PERMIT IS NEEDED FOR THE CAMPGROUND ITSELF — that is only for backcountry nights. Standard park food storage rules apply. Access is by the unpaved FR 24 beyond Lake Cushman, which closes in bad weather and is frequently shut through the winter and spring
bivy.notes: The park-side alternative at the head of Lake Cushman, a few miles beyond Big Creek. For the climbing in this zone it is a SECOND-CHOICE CONTINGENCY rather than a plan: it is further from the Ellinor and Washington trailheads than Big Creek, it costs more because of the park entrance fee, and the road in is less dependable. It earns its place for two reasons. It is the entry area named on the permit for Upper Lena Lake, so a party collecting or sorting out a park wilderness permit may already be dealing with this side of the boundary. And it is the fallback with real amenities when the Forest Service campgrounds below Ellinor are full on a summer weekend, which they routinely are. Worth knowing that the developed area has had extended seasonal closures in recent years, so confirm it is open before committing to the drive.

bivy.name: Lena Lake designated sites
bivy.capacity: Large by Olympic standards — roughly 28 to 29 numbered sites strung along the west and north shores, with a couple more on the east side; two pit toilets. It is the biggest backcountry camp in this zone and it still fills on summer weekends
bivy.water: Reliable. The lake itself, and the inlet creeks at the north end. Filter or treat everything — this is a heavily used shoreline
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass required to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit, no reservation and no fee for the sites themselves — it is Forest Service ground, first come first served. Camping is restricted to the numbered sites. Wilderness rules apply once you leave the lake basin: stoves only, no campfires, and a party limit of twelve. Plan on cooking on a stove at the lake as well
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the whole Hamma Hamma side and the single most useful site in this zone. Three easy miles and about 1,300 ft of gain on a wide graded trail from the road, so a party can leave the car after work and be in camp before dark, which is exactly how most Brothers and Mount Stone trips are staged. From here two entirely separate objectives open up: north into the Valley of the Silent Men for The Brothers, and west and up for Upper Lena Lake and the traverse toward Mount Stone. Being outside Olympic National Park is the point — no quota, no reservation, no fee, so it is the fallback when the park permits above it are gone. The cost is crowding and noise; this is a family backpacking destination as much as a climbers' camp, and the shoreline shows it. Snow-free and usable most of the year, which makes it a genuine early-season and late-season base when everything higher is buried.

bivy.water: Reliable. The lake itself, and the inlet creeks at the north end. Filter or treat everything — this is a heavily used shoreline
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass required to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. bivy.name: The Brothers climbers camp, Valley of the Silent Men
bivy.capacity: A scatter of flat, obvious tent spots in old-growth forest beside the creek, generally reported at around half a dozen usable pitches, informal rather than numbered
bivy.water: Reliable while the creek runs. The East Fork of Lena Creek is right beside the pitches, and this is the last dependable water — carry everything you need for the climb from here, because the couloir and the upper mountain hold none
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. bivy.name: Upper Lena Lake

bivy.name: Lake of the Angels

Parties heading for Columbia often sleep here instead and accept the longer approach in the morning, and it is a sensible bail if the boot path east of the pass is still snowed and the Twin Lakes descent looks like a bad idea. It is also the practical camp for anything on the Silvertip side of the pass. Snow lingers around the lake into early summer and the pass itself holds it longest. Fires are out, so carry a stove.

bivy.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
bivy.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.
bivy.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
bivy.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.

bivy.name: Royal Lake
bivy.capacity: Ten designated sites, and only two of them will take more than a single tent. One separate group site holds roughly seven to twelve people and has to be booked as a group site. That is the entire overnight capacity of the lake basin, which is why permits go so fast.
bivy.water: The lake and the outlet creek run all season. Filter or treat; this is a heavily used basin and the shoreline is fragile.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required, and Royal Basin is one of the park's named quota areas. Essentially the whole quota is reservable in advance through the federal recreation booking system, with the summer block released in a single mid-April drop for the mid-May through mid-October season; there is no same-day walk-up window, so a party that turns up without a permit has no legal camp. Expect a flat per-permit reservation charge plus a per-adult, per-night fee, with under-sixteens free and an annual wilderness pass available if you camp here often. Dates outside the online season are arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office. Hard-sided bear canisters are required, and loaners are sometimes available on a first-come basis when you collect the permit. Every camp along Royal Creek and up through the meadows and the basin sits inside the same reservation, so there is no legal way to sneak a night lower down without one.
bivy.notes: This is the front door to the whole Needles group and the default answer for anyone climbing Deception, Clark, Johnson, Walkinshaw, The Incisor or Sundial. It sits about seven miles and two and a half thousand feet from the Upper Dungeness trailhead, up the Dungeness and then the Royal Creek fork, which is walkable with a heavy pack in an afternoon. The honest trade is this: Royal Lake is comfortable, has real designated tent pads and is where the permit system actually issues sites, but it leaves you an extra mile and roughly five hundred to a thousand feet of loose boot path below the upper basin every single climbing morning. On a Needles day that difference is real, because the rock above the basin is dirty and slow and you want to be off it before the afternoon. Parties that only want one peak, or that have anyone who would rather not sleep at six thousand feet on gravel, are right to stay here. Snow lingers in the basin into July in a normal year and the mosquitoes at the lake are notorious through midsummer, which is another argument for going higher. Book the moment the reservation window opens; this is one of the hardest permits on the peninsula to get on a weekend.

bivy.name: Upper Royal Basin
bivy.capacity: No numbered sites at all. Camping is permitted only on bare ground, gravel bars and rock, so the practical capacity is a handful of parties spread across the gravel beside the tarns. Two of the larger gravel bars near the upper tarn are the usual choice for a group.
bivy.water: Tarns and snowmelt streams through the basin. Late in a dry summer the upper tarns can drop and go stagnant, so check the inlet streams rather than dipping from still water, and be prepared to carry from lower in the basin in September.
bivy.permit: Same Olympic National Park quota permit as Royal Lake, booked as the upper basin rather than the lake. All the same conditions apply: advance reservation only, mid-April release for the summer season, per-permit and per-person-per-night charges, and mandatory hard-sided bear canisters. Because there are no constructed sites, the leave-no-trace rules here are enforced in earnest: no camping on vegetation or meadow, no fires, and the park expects you to be on durable surface only. Anyone found camped on the heather is the reason this basin nearly lost overnight use.
bivy.notes: This is the climbers' camp, three quarters of a mile to a mile above the lake on an unmaintained way trail that gains around five hundred to a thousand feet. It puts you at the foot of the west wall of the basin, which is the east side of The Needles, and it is the difference between a reasonable day and a very long one on Deception, Clark, Johnson, The Incisor and Sundial. It is also the working base for Mystery, which is reached over the divide out of the head of the basin, and for Fricaba, which is a comparatively easy scramble from here and a common warm-up or bad-weather substitute. What you pay for the position: exposed camping on gravel with no trees, weather that arrives with no warning, colder nights, and a fiddly load carry up the boot path in the evening. What you get: fewer people, far fewer mosquitoes, and a start that puts you on the loose ground above the basin while it is still frozen together rather than after the sun has been on it for two hours. Snow covers the upper basin well into July most years, which is often an advantage for the approach gullies and a nuisance for finding bare ground to pitch on. If the basin is still largely snow-covered, camp on a gravel bar that has melted out rather than on snow over vegetation.

bivy.name: Camp Handy
bivy.capacity: An open three-sided shelter with log benches plus several tent sites scattered through the riverside meadow. Comfortably takes a few parties, and rarely full outside a summer weekend. No privy.
bivy.water: The Dungeness river runs right past the camp all year. Reliable.
bivy.permit: Outside the national park. This is Olympic National Forest, inside the Buckhorn Wilderness, so there is no park wilderness permit, no quota and no nightly fee. You do need a valid recreation parking pass on the vehicle at the Upper Dungeness trailhead. Bear canisters are not legally required on forest land here but food does need protecting, and if any part of your trip crosses into the park you will be carrying one anyway.
bivy.notes: A low, sheltered, permit-free camp about three miles up the Upper Dungeness trail, and the most useful fallback in the whole zone. It does not serve The Needles: Royal Basin branches off well below it and Camp Handy is on the wrong fork. What it does is give you a legal, free, roofed place to sleep when the Royal Basin quota is gone, when you arrive too late to start the Royal Creek climb, or when the weather is bad enough that a night in the trees beats a night on gravel at five and a half thousand feet. It is also the natural first night for anyone approaching Fricaba the long way, by Boulder Shelter and Constance Pass. At barely three thousand feet in old growth it is warm, wet and buggy in early summer, and it commits you to a very big day if you try to use it as a climbing base for anything on the divide. Treat it as staging, not as a base camp.

bivy.name: Boulder Shelter
bivy.capacity: A solid timber shelter with a table and bench, plus several tent sites among the boulders at the foot of the avalanche path. A few parties at most. No privy.
bivy.water: Creek water close by, though the flow drops noticeably by late summer. Fill before you commit to the climb toward Home Lake, where the next reliable source is a long way on.
bivy.permit: Still national forest and still inside the Buckhorn Wilderness, so no park permit, no quota and no fee, just a recreation parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary is crossed on the way to Home Lake, and from that point an Olympic National Park wilderness permit and a bear canister are required, so if you intend to sleep beyond here get the permit before you leave the road.
bivy.notes: About six miles up the Upper Dungeness trail, sitting under a huge avalanche chute where the trail junctions meet, at just under five thousand feet. This is the crossroads camp for the eastern half of the zone: from here the trail climbs to Home Lake and Constance Pass, which is the alternative and much less crowded way at Fricaba. It is permit-free, which matters a great deal in a zone where the good camps are rationed months in advance. It is not a Needles camp and no amount of enthusiasm makes it one. Also worth knowing before you plan around it: the stretch above here toward Home Lake is far more primitive than the trail below, with brush, blowdown and at least one crossing that will get you wet, so budget more time than the mileage suggests. The shelter is genuinely useful in bad weather, which is not something most of the alpine options in this zone can offer.

bivy.name: Home Lake
bivy.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp at the lake, room for a few parties. Nothing like Royal Lake's capacity, but it also sees a fraction of the traffic.
bivy.water: The lake, immediately at camp. Reliable through the season.
bivy.permit: Inside Olympic National Park, so an Olympic National Park wilderness permit is required, but Home Lake is NOT one of the quota areas. Reserve through the federal recreation booking system with the usual per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee; because it carries no quota, availability is generally straightforward even in midsummer, which is precisely why it is worth knowing about. Hard-sided bear canisters are required, as they are throughout park wilderness.
bivy.notes: Just over nine miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead, a little over five thousand three hundred feet, and only a few hundred feet below Constance Pass. This is the second door to Fricaba, and the reason it is in this list at all: if the Royal Basin quota is unobtainable, Fricaba can still be climbed from this side without competing for a rationed permit. It is a genuinely long walk in, with the primitive brushy section above Boulder Shelter to negotiate, so it costs you most of a day. It gives you a quiet alpine lake with real water and real shelter from wind, at a height that leaves a sensible summit day. It does nothing at all for The Needles or the Royal Basin peaks, which sit over a major divide from here. Snow holds around the lake and the pass into July. Parties combining Fricaba with Mount Constance frequently use this camp, which is worth remembering when you are guessing at how busy it will be.

bivy.name: Cedar Lake
bivy.capacity: A small high basin with room for a few parties on durable ground. Unmaintained access, so it sees very little traffic and there is no infrastructure to speak of.
bivy.water: The lake. Reliable, and the only dependable source high on this side of Gray Wolf Ridge.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; not a quota area, so it can normally be booked without a scramble for dates. Standard per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee, and a hard-sided bear canister is required. Note that the access is a primitive spur beyond the maintained trail and stock is not allowed on it.
bivy.notes: This is the only overnight in the zone that meaningfully serves the Gray Wolf Ridge crest, including the north end of the Needles ridge at Walkinshaw. It sits at about five thousand three hundred feet in a basin on the Gray Wolf side, reached up the upper Gray Wolf river from the Slab Camp trailhead on an unmaintained final section. Be clear-eyed about the cost: it is a long, remote walk in, well over ten miles, on a trail with a missing river bridge that pushes everyone onto the Slab Camp approach, and it is a completely different road and trailhead from Royal Basin. Almost nobody climbs Baldy or Gray Wolf Ridge from here, because both are done car to car in a long day from the steep Maynard Burn way trail on the Dungeness side, with no camp involved and no permit needed. Cedar Lake earns its place for the party doing the full ridge traverse, or wanting the Gray Wolf approach to Walkinshaw, or simply wanting solitude in a zone where the popular basin is rationed. If you only want to stand on Baldy and Gray Wolf Ridge, do not come here.

bivy.name: Cameron Basin
bivy.capacity: Several backcountry sites in the basin below Cameron Pass. Modest but usually adequate; the basin is on a well-travelled loop, so summer weekends can be busier than the remoteness suggests.
bivy.water: Cameron Creek and its feeders through the basin. Reliable through the climbing season.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; Cameron Basin itself is not a quota area, so it books readily. The catch is the approach: if you come the sensible way from Obstruction Point you pass through Grand and Badger Valleys, which ARE a quota area with reservations in effect through the high summer, so a night at Grand or Moose Lake on the way in has to be booked separately and early. Bear canisters are required throughout. Everything is reserved through the federal recreation booking system with the standard per-permit charge and per-adult nightly fee.
bivy.notes: This is the working base for Mount Cameron, which is climbed from Cameron Pass just above the basin, and it is the western end of this zone rather than part of the Needles group at all. Two ways in and they are very different. From Obstruction Point it is a high, scenic and long day over Grand Pass and down into the basin, and it depends entirely on the Obstruction Point road, a rough high-elevation dirt road that typically does not open until well into July and closes with the first snow of autumn; if that road is shut, this approach does not exist. From the south it is reached from Dose Meadows over Lost Pass, which is short in distance and brutally steep, but getting to Dose Meadows means the whole washed-out Dosewallips walk first. Nothing about this camp helps you on The Needles, and a party trying to combine Cameron with Deception in one trip is really planning two trips. Snow lies late in the basin and on Cameron Pass, and the descent off Grand Pass wants a dry day.

bivy.name: Dose Meadows
bivy.capacity: Several sites spread through the meadow area, plus stock use in season. It is a junction camp on a long loop, so it is rarely empty and rarely crowded.
bivy.water: The infant Dosewallips river runs through the meadows. Reliable.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; not a quota area, so it is normally available. Standard per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee through the federal recreation booking system, and a hard-sided bear canister is required. There is no permit or fee for the road-walk section below the park boundary, but you do need somewhere legal to leave the car at the closure.
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Claywood, and the southern base for Mount Cameron by way of Lost Pass and Cameron Pass. It sits at about four thousand four hundred and seventy feet at the head of the Dosewallips, and the single fact that dominates any plan built around it is the road. The Dosewallips road has been cut by a washout for over two decades and is not being rebuilt, so you start with roughly five and a half miles of old roadbed before the trail proper, and the meadows are then somewhere around seventeen to nineteen miles from where you actually park. Bicycles are permitted on the roadbed as far as the old ranger station at the wilderness boundary, which removes a meaningful chunk of that and is worth the hassle of hauling a bike. Realistically this is a two-day approach each way for most parties, which puts Claywood firmly in the category of a four to five day objective rather than a weekend. The alternative doors are Gray Wolf Pass from the Gray Wolf river, or the long way round from Obstruction Point, and neither is short. Claywood itself has no established camp of its own: parties climb it from the meadows or bivouac wherever they get to on the ridge, and there is no designated high camp to book.

bivy.name: Camp Handy

bivy.water: The Dungeness river runs right past the camp all year. Reliable.
bivy.permit: Outside the national park. This is Olympic National Forest, inside the Buckhorn Wilderness, so there is no park wilderness permit, no quota and no nightly fee. You do need a valid recreation parking pass on the vehicle at the Upper Dungeness trailhead. Bear canisters are not legally required on forest land here but food does need protecting, and if any part of your trip crosses into the park you will be carrying one anyway.

bivy.name: Boulder Shelter
bivy.capacity: A solid timber shelter with a table and bench, plus several tent sites among the boulders at the foot of the avalanche path. A few parties at most. No privy.
bivy.water: Creek water close by, though the flow drops noticeably by late summer. Fill before you commit to the climb toward Home Lake, where the next reliable source is a long way on.
bivy.permit: Still national forest and still inside the Buckhorn Wilderness, so no park permit, no quota and no fee, just a recreation parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary is crossed on the way to Home Lake, and from that point an Olympic National Park wilderness permit and a bear canister are required, so if you intend to sleep beyond here get the permit before you leave the road.
bivy.notes: About six miles up the Upper Dungeness trail, sitting under a huge avalanche chute where the trail junctions meet, at just under five thousand feet. This is the crossroads camp for the eastern half of the zone: from here the trail climbs to Home Lake and Constance Pass, which is the alternative and much less crowded way at Fricaba. The shelter is genuinely useful in bad weather, which is not something most of the alpine options in this zone can offer.

bivy.name: Home Lake
bivy.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp at the lake, room for a few parties. Nothing like Royal Lake's capacity, but it also sees a fraction of the traffic.
bivy.water: The lake, immediately at camp. Reliable through the season.
bivy.permit: Inside Olympic National Park, so an Olympic National Park wilderness permit is required, but Home Lake is NOT one of the quota areas. bivy.notes: Just over nine miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead, a little over five thousand three hundred feet, and only a few hundred feet below Constance Pass. bivy.name: Cedar Lake
bivy.capacity: A small high basin with room for a few parties on durable ground. Unmaintained access, so it sees very little traffic and there is no infrastructure to speak of.
bivy.water: The lake. Reliable, and the only dependable source high on this side of Gray Wolf Ridge.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; not a quota area, so it can normally be booked without a scramble for dates. Standard per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee, and a hard-sided bear canister is required. Note that the access is a primitive spur beyond the maintained trail and stock is not allowed on it.
bivy.notes: This is the only overnight in the zone that meaningfully serves the Gray Wolf Ridge crest, including the north end of the Needles ridge at Walkinshaw. It sits at about five thousand three hundred feet in a basin on the Gray Wolf side, reached up the upper Gray Wolf river from the Slab Camp trailhead on an unmaintained final section. Be clear-eyed about the cost: it is a long, remote walk in, well over ten miles, on a trail with a missing river bridge that pushes everyone onto the Slab Camp approach, and it is a completely different road and trailhead from Royal Basin. bivy.name: Cameron Basin

bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; Cameron Basin itself is not a quota area, so it books readily. Bear canisters are required throughout. Everything is reserved through the federal recreation booking system with the standard per-permit charge and per-adult nightly fee.

Snow lies late in the basin and on Cameron Pass, and the descent off Grand Pass wants a dry day.

bivy.name: Dose Meadows
bivy.capacity: Several sites spread through the meadow area, plus stock use in season. It is a junction camp on a long loop, so it is rarely empty and rarely crowded.
bivy.water: The infant Dosewallips river runs through the meadows. Reliable.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; not a quota area, so it is normally available. Standard per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee through the federal recreation booking system, and a hard-sided bear canister is required. There is no permit or fee for the road-walk section below the park boundary, but you do need somewhere legal to leave the car at the closure.
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Claywood, and the southern base for Mount Cameron by way of Lost Pass and Cameron Pass. The alternative doors are Gray Wolf Pass from the Gray Wolf river, or the long way round from Obstruction Point, and neither is short. Claywood itself has no established camp of its own: parties climb it from the meadows or bivouac wherever they get to on the ridge, and there is no designated high camp to book.

bivy.name: Boulder Shelter
bivy.capacity: A solid timber shelter with a table and bench, plus several tent sites among the boulders at the foot of the avalanche path. A few parties at most. No privy.
bivy.water: Creek water close by, though the flow drops noticeably by late summer. Fill before you commit to the climb toward Home Lake, where the next reliable source is a long way on.
bivy.permit: Still national forest and still inside the Buckhorn Wilderness, so no park permit, no quota and no fee, just a recreation parking pass at the trailhead. bivy.notes: About six miles up the Upper Dungeness trail, sitting under a huge avalanche chute where the trail junctions meet, at just under five thousand feet. bivy.name: Home Lake
bivy.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp at the lake, room for a few parties. Nothing like Royal Lake's capacity, but it also sees a fraction of the traffic.

bivy.name: Cedar Lake
bivy.capacity: A small high basin with room for a few parties on durable ground. Unmaintained access, so it sees very little traffic and there is no infrastructure to speak of.
bivy.water: The lake. Reliable, and the only dependable source high on this side of Gray Wolf Ridge.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; not a quota area, so it can normally be booked without a scramble for dates. Standard per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee, and a hard-sided bear canister is required. Note that the access is a primitive spur beyond the maintained trail and stock is not allowed on it.
bivy.notes: This is the only overnight in the zone that meaningfully serves the Gray Wolf Ridge crest, including the north end of the Needles ridge at Walkinshaw. It sits at about five thousand three hundred feet in a basin on the Gray Wolf side, reached up the upper Gray Wolf river from the Slab Camp trailhead on an unmaintained final section. bivy.name: Cameron Basin
bivy.capacity: Several backcountry sites in the basin below Cameron Pass. Modest but usually adequate; the basin is on a well-travelled loop, so summer weekends can be busier than the remoteness suggests.

bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; Cameron Basin itself is not a quota area, so it books readily. The catch is the approach: if you come the sensible way from Obstruction Point you pass through Grand and Badger Valleys, which ARE a quota area with reservations in effect through the high summer, so a night at Grand or Moose Lake on the way in has to be booked separately and early. bivy.notes: This is the working base for Mount Cameron, which is climbed from Cameron Pass just above the basin, and it is the western end of this zone rather than part of the Needles group at all.
